sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **August Declaration of 1917**: Edwin Montagu announced the gradual introduction of responsible government in India as an integral part of the British Empire.
• **Dyarchy at Provinces**: Executive departments were divided into **Transferred** (administered by ministers responsible to the legislative council) and **Reserved** subjects (administered by the Governor and his executive council).
• **Bicameral Legislature at Center**: The Indian Legislative Council was replaced by a bicameral system consisting of the **Council of State** (Upper House) and the **Central Legislative Assembly** (Lower House).
• **Key Metric / Factor**: Franchise was heavily restricted based on property, tax, or educational qualifications, covering barely 3% of the population for the provincial assemblies.

items.definition: A system of dual governance introduced in provincial subjects, splitting administration into Reserved and Transferred portfolios, which suffered from inherent friction and financial control issues.
System of separate electorates initiated for Muslims under Minto-Morley and aggressively expanded under Montford Reforms to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians, and Europeans.
The Upper House created under the 1919 Act with a tenure of 5 years, having a majority of official members and restricted elite franchise.
The Lower House with a 3-year tenure, having a majority of elected members, though the Governor-General retained overriding veto and certification powers.

items.title: Major Geographical Distribution / Regional Hubs
items.content:
• **British Provinces**: Dyarchy was applied across major provinces like Madras, Bombay, Bengal, United Provinces, Punjab, Bihar & Orissa, and Central Provinces.
• **Princely States**: Kept outside the direct purview of provincial dyarchy, though a consultative **Chamber of Princes (Narendra Mandal)** was established in 1921.

items.title: Challenges, Reforms & Forward Strategy
items.content:
• **Bottlenecks / Issues**: Financial stringency of Transferred departments, ministerial dependence on Governors, and failure to meet nationalist aspirations.
• **Policy Interventions**: Led directly to the boycott by Congress, the Non-Cooperation Movement, and the subsequent appointment of the Simon Commission in 1927.

items.title: Mnemonic for Transferred Subjects
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym / Phrase**: **HALE** (Health, Agriculture, Local Self-Government, Education).
• **Decoded Meaning**: The core welfare subjects handed over to Indian ministers under provincial dyarchy.
• **Prelims Exam Value**: Instantly differentiates Transferred subjects from Reserved subjects like Police and Finance.

items.title: Retention Rule of Thumb
items.content: • **Core Formula / Rule**: 1909 = Morley-Minto (Separate Electorates for Muslims); 1919 = Mont-Ford (Dyarchy + Bicameralism + Expanded Electorates); 1935 = Provincial Autonomy + Federal Court.

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC frequently states that the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms introduced adult universal suffrage or complete responsible government at the center. Both statements are false; franchise was extremely restricted, and the center had no responsible government.

Mains Value Addition: Critically evaluate the Montford Reforms using the phrase 'too little, too late' and highlight how institutionalizing separate electorates deepened communal fissures, ultimately paving the way for partition.

keyTakeaways: The Montford Reforms introduced dyarchy in provinces, dividing subjects into Reserved and Transferred categories.
A bicameral central legislature was established with direct elections for the Central Legislative Assembly under a restricted franchise.
Communal electorates were significantly expanded, institutionalizing identity-based politics in India.
